raw_response.country: Canada (with a brief secondary policy comparison to the United States)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines safe drinking water and wastewater/sanitation service access and infrastructure conditions on First Nations reserves in Canada, including drinking water advisories and household water delivery modes.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — extensively discusses federal constitutional jurisdiction under the Indian Act, the absence of provincial or federal statutory drinking water regulation on reserves, Bills S-11 and S-8, AANDC annual contribution agreements, the 80/20 O&M cost-sharing requirement, and Indigenous water governance. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Yes at the policy-discussion level (though mixed with unanalysed macro-governance, colonial history, and community-capacity theory) — specifically discusses rule-type regulatory, administrative-contracting, and cost-recovery mechanisms directly governing reserve water systems (non-application of provincial drinking water regulations and enforcement on reserves, annual contribution agreement reapplication/reporting burdens, 80/20 O&M cost-sharing and user-fee affordability, and third-party utility liability rules), but only via secondary policy commentary rather than empirical analysis. Both plain and narrow readings still result in exclusion because the paper fails Criteria 3 and 5.
criterion_notes.c3: No — this is a narrative policy overview and conceptual essay (presenting a theoretical model of human, physical, and social capital for sustainable development) rather than an empirical study with identifiable data/methods or a systematic empirical synthesis. Although pages 10-11 include seven brief illustrative quotes from 'several focus groups that included residents of northern First Nation communities,' the paper contains no methods section and reports zero methodological details (no number of focus groups, sample size, community selection, dates, interview guide, or analytic method), relying throughout on secondary government reports, AFN policy briefs, and conceptual commentary.
criterion_notes.c4: Unclear — cites secondary aggregate figures from Health Canada, the Auditor General, and a 2009 EKOS survey on reserve drinking water advisories, system risk ratings, and household delivery modes (piped, cistern, well), plus brief anecdotal focus-group remarks on source vulnerability and pipe installation, but reports no primary empirical service-access outcome linked to an analyzed governance exposure.
criterion_notes.c5: No — lacks an identifiable empirical study design and does not provide sufficient methodological information to identify a primary study population/sample or an empirically analyzed exposure-outcome relationship.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes — full text is in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: As of August 2012, 119 communities, out of over 600 First Nations communities in Canada, were under water advisories requiring residents to either boil their water or to heed ‘do not drink warnings’ (Health Canada, 2012).

The mechanism used by AANDC and Health Canada is ‘contribution agreements’, which are contracts for every service provided that outline the funding to be given and responsibility of the community in the program. Communities were required to make many reports on the use of the funds.

It is easy to see that for most communities even 20% of operating costs may be out of reach. The issue is that the communities have to take money out of other programs, education or child welfare for example, in order to make up the 20% (Morales 2006).

To understand why this paradox and problem persists, this article will work through the issues and nuances that have created unsafe drinking water on reserve, proposed remedies, and policy implications.

As part of our study, we conducted several focus groups that included residents of northern First Nation communities. These groups helped to give our team a clearer understanding of how First Nations individuals view water issues around them.
Only 55% of the homes surveyed had water delivered to their home; 19% used a cistern and 17% used wells. Others had no sources listed.

raw_response.exposure: Federal vs. provincial drinking water regulatory gap on reserves, Indian Act governance, Bills S-11 and S-8, AANDC annual contribution agreements, and the 80/20 operating and maintenance cost-sharing rule (discussed via secondary policy documents and conceptual commentary)
raw_response.outcome: Secondary descriptive statistics on reserve drinking water advisories, medium/high-risk water and wastewater systems, and household water delivery modes (piped, cistern, well from EKOS 2009); no primary empirical service-access outcome reported
raw_response.population_and_sample: First Nations reserve communities in Canada discussed at a national policy level; illustrative quotes from an unreported number of focus groups and participants in unspecified northern First Nation communities
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (no empirical evidence with identifiable data/methods; narrative policy overview and conceptual essay, not an empirical study or systematic synthesis). While the article examines safe drinking water and wastewater challenges on First Nations reserves in Canada (c1=yes) and discusses regulatory gaps, annual contribution agreements, 80/20 O&M cost-sharing rules, and proposed federal legislation (c2=yes at topic level under both plain and narrow readings), it has no methods section, no identifiable empirical study design, and no reported sample size, site selection, data collection, or analytic procedure for the brief illustrative focus-group quotes inserted on pages 10-11, nor does it empirically analyze a governance exposure against a primary service-access outcome (c3=no, c5=no).
raw_response.study_design: Narrative policy overview and conceptual essay (with uncharacterized illustrative focus group quotes; no empirical methods reported)
